# Design envelope

## Batch 187: existing lightmap parity entries and opaque visibility

Batch 54 already supplies indexed mesh baking on UV1 (the second UV set), progressive WebGPU compute with a live
texture and AbortSignal, per-texel path bounces in ./global, and dominant-direction maps in ./directional. No duplicate
entries were added. The opaque visibility correction changes ./global from 7,770 to 7,781 gzip bytes (minified entry,
bare imports external); its existing 8,007-byte ceiling holds. Existing mesh/gpu/directional entries measure
3,128/7,722/4,215 bytes by the same method. Core and stage sources are unchanged.

Opaque quad backs now block area-light shadow segments and diffuse paths in both quad and path modes. Their back
sides supply no emission or reflected light. This matches the existing direct point/spot/directional baker's two-sided
shadow visibility. Alpha omission and glass transport retain their explicit visibility rules. Surface transport still
uses the stored texel's front normal and diffuse radiance; it does not add two-sided emission or a new material model.
The historical Cornell loss remains open as detailed in known-bugs.md; this change makes no accuracy-parity claim.

Progressive splat cancellation rejects pending consumers and requests async
iterator return without waiting indefinitely for producer IO or cleanup. The
producer owns external work; its return implementation must release that work.
Aborting between buffered batches prevents further decoded records. See
docs/splats-progressive.md for exact cancellation regressions and sources.

Batch 175 job 1: sciviz/omezarr opens OME-NGFF 0.4/Zarr2 and 0.5/Zarr3 multiscales with named spatial/time/channel axes, composed dataset/group scale and translation, one bricked source per stored level, and a dyadic renderer adapter. Reads retain source coordinates; stored LOD samples use nearest-neighbour physical-coordinate sampling, not a claim that arbitrary stored pyramids equal on-the-fly box averaging. Supply volume.bounds and a known range when attaching its source to brickedVolume. Each level also exposes its existing ZarrArray for typed exact-region reads. Rendering is float32; 64-bit integer Zarr reads use the existing Float64 representation and are exact only through 2^53. Arrays are 2D through 5D; renderer volumes need three nondegenerate dimensions. Unknown nonsingleton axes require selection before use. Channel and image default to zero; frame comes from BrickRequest. No IO or GPU allocations occur on import.

HTTP/S3 stores support absolute and suffix Range reads, credential headers, missing-key-only 404 handling and lifetime/request cancellation. Defaults: maxBytes and maxDecodedBytes 67,108,864 bytes each, channel 0, image 0, 16 cached Zarr shard indexes and no cached payloads. A server ignoring Range may return at most maxBytes. Shard indexes use bytes (either endian) plus optional CRC32C; inner shapes must divide shard shape. Standard one-level sharding is supported; nested sharding and codecs outside the documented pipeline reject. Blosc1 supports memcpy, BloscLZ, LZ4/LZ4HC, zlib and zstd, byte and bit shuffle; extended Blosc2 filter pipelines and legacy Snappy reject. Zstd dictionary frames retain the existing decoder's explicit unsupported result. LZ4 includes numcodecs length-prefixed blocks and N5 Java streams with 28-bit seeded xxHash checksums. N5 fixed-size scalar blocks support raw, gzip, bzip2, XZ, LZ4, Blosc and zstd; variable-length/object blocks are not scalar-volume arrays. Precomputed supports raw, grayscale/RGB JPEG and compressed_segmentation, unsharded and identity-hashed sharded scales; other image/segmentation encodings and Murmur-hashed shards reject explicitly. These limits concern codec/storage variants, not silent missing-data fallbacks.

Scale evidence uses work and bytes, with no timed benchmark: a 10^12-sample synthetic array opens with zero chunk reads and a one-sample ROI reads exactly one 8-byte chunk. The three real regions each return 32,768 float32 samples (131,072 bytes), rendered as nine resident bricks in 105,040 GPU bytes on native WebGPU and the full WebGL2 layer. The original full dimensions are IDR 2048x2048x1937, N5 12000x1600x6368 and FlyEM 34427x39725x41394. This proves bounded selected-region work, not full-dataset residency or a measured speed comparison. Independent lossless IDR/N5 values match all samples exactly; existing JPEG/Pillow IDCT rounding differs by at most 1 on the recorded FlyEM sample. No lossless precision or JPEG bit-exactness claim is made for that lossy source.
API lock Day 0 (2026-11-10): core/stage are locked by package, including future entries. Other reported packages
warn in watch pending Day 1 promotion. The declaration-text gate does not prove runtime semantics or general subtype
compatibility. Only additions, trailing optional parameters and optional relaxations are recognized as compatible;
other declaration edits conservatively break. Approval binds entry, symbol, change and an eight-character SHA-1 of
the old block (review identity, not a security hash). Coverage requires resolved reports per non-alias exports entry.
See [API lock](conventions.md#api-lock) for policy, sources and regression evidence.

Batch 190 job 2: `@margoengine/oit/precise` adds PreciseOIT, 3777 B min+gzip (new from 0 B, ceiling 4033 B). Four R32F sums plus R16F revealage cost 18 bytes per pixel at 1x, 72 at 4x; five simultaneous colour attachments are required. Native WebGPU needs Engine.create's `features: ['float32-blendable']`; full WebGL2 needs EXT_float_blend and renderable R32F targets (4x R32F renderbuffers for MSAA). Missing capabilities reject before buffer allocation. No float32 filtering is required. The weighted approximation, depthScale default (camera-target distance), order default 8, material texture budget and sorted handling of transmission/custom blending/depth overrides are unchanged. No `blending` option is exposed by this entry. Float32 sums have the finite f32 range, so total weighted radiance must stay below roughly 3.4e38; the final HDR target still sets the output range. Core and stage remain 24209 B combined gzip.

Batch 190 job 1: `@margoengine/oit/peel` adds PeelOIT, 3037 B min+gzip (new from 0 B, ceiling 3293 B). It captures ten nearest distinct depths by default, adjustable with a positive safe integer `layers`; more layers cost one geometry redraw and one resolve draw each. Storage is `12 * layers + 8` bytes per pixel, 128 B/pixel at the default, independent of scene MSAA. Exact order holds at distinct raster depths; coplanar fragments share one layer and the last submitted wins. Transparent coverage is single sample even over a 4x opaque target; post FXAA works. This matches the documented rival antialiasing restriction. RGBA16F captured radiance still has a 65504 maximum. Full WebGL2 compatibility requires renderable floating targets; no fragment storage or float32 blending. Refraction, transmission/custom blending, depth overrides and particles remain on their existing paths; addEffect explicitly refuses this model-only pass. Core and stage remain unchanged at 24209 B combined gzip.

Batch 204 job 2: optional exporters/textures is 10015 B gzip (new from 0 B),
ceiling 10316 B. Resize accepts at most 16384 per side and 16777216 pixels for
input, output and horizontal intermediate (Float64 RGBA, at most 512 MiB).
WebP/AVIF/JPEG encoding requires the requested platform canvas encoder;
unsupported or silently substituted formats reject with a coded error naming
the missing MIME. Chromium 157 encoded WebP but lacked AVIF encoding in both
backend checks. PNG works without canvas for RGBA input. Native encode timeout
is 30 seconds; native quality and low-alpha canvas rounding are platform-defined.
AVIF byte input currently needs caller-decoded RGBA. AVIF uses the published
draft glTF extension contract, with optional PNG/JPEG fallback; no ratification
or portable AVIF encoder claim. Details and defaults: exporter-textures.md.

Batch 256 migration: `@margoengine/netcode/migrate` exports HostMigration and its
typed options/state. Give each peer the same schema, initial state, frame and
host (default lowest id), and reliable full-mesh Connection links. It owns and
closes these links, forwards other message kinds to earlier handlers, and uses
wire prefix 112 for migration. Up to 64 peers; checkpoint default 1 MiB, maximum
16 MiB. Initial frame defaults to 0, operation/recovery/wait timeout to 10 seconds.
Frames, sequences and authority epochs are unsigned 32-bit; create a new session
before overflow. `confirm(state, frame, { signal })` serially prepares and commits
on every connected peer and resolves only after all stored acknowledgements.
`confirmed` is a detached locally committed copy; await confirm before treating
it as globally confirmed. Exactly two committed checkpoints are retained.
Host disconnect selects the lowest surviving id, restores the newest common
checkpoint and completes a survivor acknowledgement barrier before isHost becomes
true. `handoff(target, { signal })` moves authority without leaving. Only isHost
may simulate/publish authority work; use waitForHost to resume after migration.
Abort/timeout of a publishing operation retires that session and closes its links
rather than reusing an uncertain checkpoint. Cancelling waitForHost only cancels
that wait. Trusted peers and a connected surviving full mesh are required; arbitrary
network partitions, malicious voters, durable restart and adding peers to a live
session require external membership/fencing or a fresh session. No consensus or
partition-safety claim is made. The public role-switch behavior of Photon Realtime
is covered, with explicit checkpoint replication/restoration supplied here.
New migration entry gzip is 8,351 B (previously absent), ceiling 8,607 B. Complete
checkpoint validation, two-phase replication, handoff and recovery remain in one
optional entry. Splitting them would expose protocol internals and duplicate
session lifecycle wiring. Core and stage remain 23,950 B combined gzip.

Batch 256 Rust generation: `@margoengine/netcode/generate-rust` exports
generateRust(schema.json or compiledSchema, { source? }). Output is standalone
Rust 2021 requiring Rust 1.82 or newer, with no crate dependencies. Each schema
type becomes Msg<Name>, each field f_<name>, maps BTreeMap<u32, T>, enums u32
wire indices and optionals Option<Box<T>>. Native methods encode, decode,
encode_delta, decode_delta and same use the runtime codec's wire contract and
normalized SCHEMA_HASH. f32 fields use native f32; quantized values use f64.
Encoding and decoding return margo_wire::Result, validate limits and reject
trailing bytes, invalid UTF-8, non-finite floats and malformed map/mask data.
Nesting above 256 codec calls returns an error to bound untrusted recursion.
This is a generator and native protocol codec, not a new engine Wasm bundle.
New entry gzip is 9,827 B (previously absent), ceiling 10,122 B. Schema validation,
complete codec emission and native data conversion stay together; a split would
force generator consumers to assemble a second template entry without saving
runtime application bytes. Core and stage remain unchanged.

Batch 256 presence: `@margoengine/netcode/presence` exposes RoomPresence,
PresenceStore, MemoryPresence, StorePresence, openSqlitePresence and RoomNode.
Run each node's `run({ signal })` promise and handle its rejection; `close()` or
`await using` withdraws it after in-flight heartbeat/service tasks have stopped.
Lease defaults to 10 seconds, heartbeat to 1 second (strictly shorter than lease),
IPC timeout to 5 seconds and poll interval to 20 ms. List snapshots are eventually
consistent; `sync()` refreshes them immediately. Remote reserve always executes
on the room owner and returns its endpoint and one-time join credential. Failed
or uncertain RPCs are never replayed. A cancellation after the owner claims a
request may leave its reserved seat until normal reservation expiry. Private
and full rooms remain routable by id but are hidden from public list results.
The shared-store adapter requires atomic take and expiry-aware reads. The supplied
SQLite WAL adapter uses Node's lazy built-in sqlite module and a local file shared
by processes on one host; network filesystems and multi-host SQLite are unsupported.
Implement the public store/presence contract for a network database. The control
plane is trusted server code; applications authenticate matchmaking endpoints.
Presence entry gzip is 6,219 B (new entry, previously absent), ceiling 6,475 B.
The optional entry retains the complete shared-store adapter and native SQLite
path; splitting would add another public adapter entry without reducing room
control-plane work. Core and stage stay unchanged at 23,950 B combined gzip.

Batch 256 lobby: `@margoengine/netcode/lobby` provides `LobbyRoom` and `RoomLobby`.
List results contain room id/name, detached scalar metadata, connected clients,
reserved/reconnecting seats and capacity. Name and metadata filters are exact;
locked, full and private rooms are omitted. Reservations default to 15 seconds,
accept 1..2147483647 integer milliseconds, and hold capacity through async auth.
Join with `RoomsClient.joinById(roomId, { seatToken }, joinOptions)`. Join options
come from the server reservation, and the token is consumed once after successful
authentication. Cancellation/expiry/disposal free holds. Applications expose the
lobby over their own authenticated HTTP API and protect tokens with TLS; holding
a token grants its reserved join identity. Ordinary Room subclasses can be listed
but require LobbyRoom to reserve. Entry gzip is 4,183 B (new entry, previously
absent); its size ceiling is 4,439 B. Keeping the capacity-safe reservation and
listing together avoids a second room wrapper. Core and stage are unchanged.

Compatibility compute pipeline binding counts obey `device.limits` on every
compute route. Explicit layouts count all compute-visible entries across groups,
even unused entries; external textures consume four sampled-texture slots, one
sampler and one uniform. Overflow is a validation error and async creation
rejects with `GPUPipelineError`. The complete shader readback leaf, including
validation and recovery, passes on native WebGPU and full compat. Lower-tier and
other package gaps remain separately listed. Batch 273 failure 18 entry gzip:
root 105,454 B, device 105,996 B, XR 105,896 B, tiers 105,955 B. Core + stage
remain 23,950 B; no ceiling was increased.

Verify's shadow archive store retains its 5 GiB cap and per-write oldest-first
eviction. Windows reads fresh enumeration metadata through its system .NET
runtime rather than individually statting every ordinary archive; a helper
invocation is bounded at 60 seconds. Links/directories and non-Windows platforms
retain Node stat behavior. Every insertion still inventories the full directory,
so enumeration/transfer work scales with archive count. No metadata is retained
between evictions. This changes tooling work, not engine size.

GPU lock idle reclamation defaults to three minutes. `MARGO_GPU_IDLE_MIN` may
cover a measured shader compile plus margin, capped by the command's existing
`--max` hard hold limit. It does not extend test deadlines. The lease records the
chosen millisecond window so its independent monitor uses the same bound.

Batch 234 independent caustics continuation: the optional entry is 8961 B

Core plus stage remains current main's 23950 B, below 25000 B; this job changes

Current acceptance and retained history: [caustics record](water-caustics.md).

Historical initial caustics checkpoint: `@margoengine/water/caustics` measures 8122 B
min+gzip (8378 B ceiling), absent before this optional entry. Its three RGB
flux-vector maps cost `24 * resolution ** 2 * layers` bytes: 18 MiB at the
256-square/12-slice defaults, plus captures and stack targets. Sides 32..2048,
2..32 horizontal height slices, camera-centred map width 0.1..100000 m and
explicit receiver heights -100000..100000 m. Subpixel beams use normalized
pixel-aligned box footprints; resolved triangles keep their geometry. It is a
single refractive-interface raster model with opaque depth receivers. Depthless
transparent receivers and overturning volumes are outside it. These receiver, shadow, attenuation, extreme-focus, lifecycle and visual bars
now pass; the following record preserves the earlier checkpoint status. [Research and current evidence](water-caustics.md).

Batch 213 job 1: optional `rigging/vrm0` is 6,543 B min+gzip (previously absent;

## Owned Zstd destination limits

The internal shared reader's optional destination is exclusive caller storage
until the promise settles. Its capacity adds a limit to `maxOutputSize`; it
never grows or substitutes the buffer. Returned bytes are a prefix view.
Input/output ranges must not overlap. Do not resize, detach, transfer or grow
its Wasm memory while borrowed. On rejection its contents are unspecified.
The existing 256MiB output and128MiB window defaults, dictionary refusal,
checksum verification, concatenated/skippable frames and cancellation remain.
This does not replace the shipped Basis transcoder or close its RSS losses.

[Current combined-Wasm evidence](whitepaper/results/batch-134-corpus-uploads-memory.json)

and public integration fuzz proof remains open. The same 1,296 scalar images
round-trip 131,581,656 compressed bytes on real RTX A6000 WebGPU. This is
compressed-byte transport; no sampled-pixel, full mip-chain texture or public
loader acceptance. Native WebGPU exposes no ETC2/EAC support on this adapter;
993 such images remain unproven rather than passed.

Fresh old/new processes retain all outputs on all 173 accepted scalar pairs.
Maximum Wasm high water is 17,170,432 old / 10,747,904 new bytes, with no
per-pair Wasm loss. Maximum process RSS is 112,460 old / 113,708 new KiB;
25 per-pair RSS losses remain open. RSS includes runtime/input/output and
allocator behavior; it is not just Wasm pages or peak-live allocations. The
JS adapter materializes a full Zstd level then copies it into Wasm, adding
4,194,304 bytes of duplicate raw-level storage on the diagnosed control.
No forced GC, reduced work, discarded output, tolerance or timing excuse.
The same-payload uncompressed diagnostic removes that control's RSS loss,
with 12 exact old and 12 exact new hashes, but is not a shipped fix.

## Batch 171 tracer numerical limits and size attribution

The CPU streamline step is a maximum arc step, adaptively shortened. Local error estimate is the RK4
step-doubling norm / 15, bounded by 1e-6 times current arc step; it is not a guaranteed global error bound.
Unresolved stages/turns halve; progress stops at max(1e-6 min(step, grid spacing), 32 epsilon
max(abs(position components), step)), as well as minSpeed/masks/boundaries/maxSteps. No critical-point
location, global separatrix preservation or closed-orbit classification is claimed. True cycles are retained.
/tubes remains 2,533 B gzip, /grids 23,735 B, LIC 23,461 B, flow 8,665 B. The tracer repair changes
/maths 5,389 -> 5,703 B (ceiling 5,638 -> 5,959) and root 50,303 -> 50,599 B (within 51,813).
Core/stage remains 23,924 B, below 25,000. The optional bytes buy error control and safe termination;
splitting this existing solver would complicate the synchronous API and duplicate its sampling contract.
LIC's exact 10,429 -> 23,461 B change is +13,032 B of required published-precision shared colormap
lookup/data, proven by an isolated local-history substitution with the identical measurement method.

Batch 171 tubes/ribbons CPU checkpoint: a new optional /tubes adapter reuses Margo geometry's sweep,
parallel transport, joined seam normals and flat caps. Polyline input is resampled at equal arc length:
2..16385 points, 1..16384 output steps, tube sides 3..128, at most one million wall vertices. Increase steps
for bends/radius/scalar features between output rows; polygonal self-intersection is not removed. Finite
input magnitudes are at most 1e15. Rendering positions/normals/scalars are float32. Width and radius may
reach zero but must have at least one positive input; duplicate samples and reversing cusps reject. Closed
input repeats its first point/scalar/size exactly. Physical ribbon spin integrates half streamwise curl over
travel time, with positive speeds; accumulated angle is at most 1e12 radians. Closed physical spin must be
whole full turns. Pure geometry needs no disposal; streamMeshTriangles returns an independent triangle set
for the existing mesh renderer, with output typed arrays limited to 128 MiB. No new renderer or Wasm kernel.
CPU checkpoint only: entry size, real NOAA demo, both GPU backends and final acceptance remain pending.

Batch 171 LIC (`@margoengine/sciviz/lic`): optional GPU dense convolution of regular 2D fields and affine planar
slices through regular 3D fields. Static box filter or explicit-phase periodic direction animation, with scalar
colour (default interpolated full-vector speed). Each image/noise dimension is 8..2048, independently of the
field; 1..128 midpoint samples each way, step 0.1..1 texels. Snapshot plus packed field: 128 MiB working budget;
image: 16 bytes/texel, maximum 64 MiB, also bounded by device storage limits. Samples: finite within +/-1e30
or NaN; a nonzero node must retain a component >=8*2^-126 after common scaling, so eight-neighbour
interpolation does not rely on subnormals. Local scaled norms preserve parallel tangents across 24 orders
without a nonzero speed cutoff. Slice coordinates/mappings within +/-1e15, sin(angle)^2 > 1e-8. Missing/outside texels mask rather than
bridge. Readback temporarily adds one image-sized buffer and a luminance array. No arbitrary-triangle surface
LIC, volume LIC or physical unsteady advection claim. Native sciviz/webgl2 is unsupported; the intended
backends are WebGPU and compatibility-backed WebGL2. Independent analytical box error: 1.4725853414443435e-7;
exact circular-arc error: 1.1380660922433172e-5. Both have zero backend pixel differences and exact restoration.
The NOAA demo passes both layouts/backends. The normalized pre-integration entry was 10,429 B gzip.
After main restored full published colormap precision, LIC is 23,461 B gzip, ceiling 24,165 B (was 10,517 B).
The coherent clean-source entry/network records name c1a799e75: root 50,303 B, flow 8,665 B and
native driver 4,476 B. The optional bytes preserve published colour values and the synchronous colormap API;
a lazy table split would add loading/API/deployment complexity only to reduce optional size.
Core/stage source is unchanged at 23,924 B combined gzip, with the strict 25,000 B ceiling intact.
The one full verify ran 13,769 tests: 13,765 passed; four metadata/test-fixture failures were corrected and the
affected checks pass. Package CPU/GPU, README, lint, hygiene and quality checks pass; no speed claim.

Batch 134 report 15 scalar refinement remains unaccepted: 86/98 original-source quality
pairs pass, 12 fail; both conventional and mapped R/alpha bars remain unchanged.
Draft Wasm is 168,906 B raw / 60,673 B gzip9, compared with the initial scalar
prototype's 158,873 / 57,653 B. The 3,020 gzip bytes provide both-mode endpoint

[Current scoped evidence](whitepaper/results/batch-134-scalar-refinement.json).

Owned Chromium runs under a browser host process (`scripts/support/browser-host.mjs`,
2026-11-10): the suite ends the browser through the host, is acknowledged as soon
as every process has been told to end, and waits for the kernel's teardown of the
ended processes only up to 2,000 ms, then moves on. The host waits up to 120 s more
and records any survivor in `test-results/browser-host-survivors.log`. A GPU slot can
therefore be released while the kernel is still freeing the ended browser's GPU
allocations (measured 65 ms to 1.2 s beside the batches, 8.7 s beside verify). The
30,000 ms shutdown budget and 5,000 ms process-list bound are unchanged.
Batch 56 proof continuation keeps exact outside-view RGB equality and exact
shadow-mask return statistics. The fixtures now use the supported view-clear and
camera-up APIs; no core/stage code, sample count or numerical bar changes. Fog-all
has analytic correctness evidence without a stored earlier-build image baseline.
Shader plugin disposal resolves identity through sceneOf; no rendering feature
or speed claim is introduced. Wider owner and capture acceptance remain open.

The optional TAA upscale entry is 7,112 B min+gzip versus the previous recorded
7,079 B. Its ceiling increases from 7,093 to 7,112 B under Scott's optional-package
ruling: retain camera identity, scene disposal and mainline preview diagnostics.
Splitting the synchronous camera wrapper would split identity/restoration
ownership or require a loader. Core plus stage remains 23,924 B. All shader
entries fit their unchanged ceilings; shader root is 18,489 B, raw 14,270 B,
scene pass 12,476 B. These are byte measurements, not performance results.

GPU `run` and `enqueue` accept GPU leaves only; known CPU aggregators cannot be
overridden, and unclassified GPU leaves require a logged `--gpu` reason. New
clients hold one slot per canonical worktree or owner lane prefix. Admission is
FIFO among eligible lanes, bypassing requests whose lane already holds a slot.
Old clients interoperate, but their missing lane metadata limits enforcement.
Windows WDDM GPU Engine snapshots cover the holder process tree every 30 seconds
with uint64 strings/BigInt, a 45-second query limit and 5-second termination
allowance. Three minutes of stable complete idle samples trigger confirmed,
identity-pinned tree termination and own-token release. Unknown data, resets,
PID reuse or gaps above 90 seconds prevent idle reclaim; other platforms retain
the normal hold timeout. Sampling can miss short-lived GPU children between
observations. Status distinguishes busy, idle and unknown; slotsUsed/3 counts
leases, not GPU utilization. Free-slot wait totals integrate scheduler-observed
transitions, including requests blocked by the lane rule; they do not trace
legacy events continuously. CPU-only regressions and owned Windows sleeper
termination prove policy and lifecycle, not GPU speed or continuous tracing.
Queue terminal observation bounds owner handle draining at 30 seconds; waiter
withdrawal has a separate 30-second mutex cleanup bound to close wait accounting.

and 22 selected Node tests; 40 of 98 file/target source-quality pairs fail.
The unchanged conventional and R/alpha bars both apply. Draft Wasm is 158,873 B
raw / 57,653 B gzip9; this is not final entry, peak-memory or speed acceptance.

GPU exclusive policy is checked before verify builds: tracked production source
and package scripts are scanned for literal CLI/environment/API requests.
Computed commands are checked at runtime; the syntax gate does not evaluate
programs. Synthetic fixtures, lock/queue internals and historical whitepaper
results are outside the static scan, with runtime admission still enforced.
Detached queue observers read immutable numbered status revisions. Older single-
file records are still readable; observers need the new scripts for new revision
records. Holder and waiter lock formats remain compatible with older clients.

Owned Chromium shutdown lists its processes before client disconnect, then ends
them through the host. A process-list read still has its five-second bound and
shutdown retains the 30-second budget. The regressions in
`tests/browser-teardown.test.js` and `tests/browser-host.test.js` prove ordering and
the bounded hand-off, not a GPU speed or universal driver-shutdown guarantee.

Sciviz review validation records are regenerated as a pair from one built revision:
`node examples/package-benchmarks/entry-sizes.mjs`, then
`node scripts/basic-scene-network.mjs`. The latter captures a real GPU-backed
basic scene. Both records retain their actual commit and packages-dirty flag;
`tests/sizes-page.test.js` rejects a mismatched pair or an unmeasured lazy file.
This measures byte counts only during the deferred speed phase. The core + stage
ceiling remains 25,000 B; the reviewed build measures 23,950 B gzip.

Sciviz `/flow` supplies fixed-step RK4 pathlines/streaklines and GPU particles/trails on regular 2D/3D grids
with linear temporal interpolation. Adaptive error control and extrapolation are not supplied. The default
10,000-step budget accepts 1 to 1,000,000; at most 4,096 frames. CPU input copies plus
output/final-copy/scratch are capped at 128 MiB, excluding caller input and module overhead. Copy/integration
chunks are 16,384 samples/128 steps. The feature-local Wasm is 7,916 bytes, capped below 16,000 raw and 8,000 gzip
by CPU tests. It loads lazily per call; root/fallback do not load it. Samples are float32 and arithmetic/output
float64. Streaklines reuse one instance/field copy for 1..4096 ordered releases, returning observation-time
endpoints and NaN gaps for invalid/unfinished releases. GPU transport is forward only; each RK stage uses
float32 normalised coordinates/velocities, with four stages and an accepted-endpoint validity check. The
analytic GPU/CPU test bound is 0.0002 distance units on its stated fields, not a general error guarantee.
GPU layer creation copies fields; its 1..1000000 particles and 2..256 history samples (defaults 1024/32)
must fit 128 MiB of GPU buffers and device binding/buffer limits. CPU copies are additional. Bounds/widths
must survive float32; normalised velocities and step-times-velocity are at most float32 max/16 for arithmetic
headroom. Lifetime defaults to 10 time units, expires at step endpoints and fixed-seed respawn defaults true.
Width defaults 2 device pixels (positive, at most 64), opacity 0.8, sRGB colour #7ddcff. Heads are squares;
history fades quadratically and never bridges respawn generations. Uniform/random/rake/region seed layouts
are deterministic for a given seed/partition on one backend; cross-device bit identity is unclaimed.
Actual device replacement replays accepted partitions, bounded by maxSteps; advance/draw do no position
readback. Explicit readPositions has a 30000 ms default timeout. WebGPU and WebGL2 compatibility pass
numeric/pixel/lifecycle tests; native WebGL2 flow remains pending with batch 181. NOAA daily means do not
establish observed tracks or forecast accuracy. The official Moving wind example preserves these limitations.
The `/flow` JavaScript entry is 8,665 B gzip (raised optional ceiling 8,854 B);
the previous CPU-only size was 2,130 B (ceiling 2,386 B). Root remains 36,916 B, driver 4,476 B, Wasm 7,916 raw /
3,585 gzip B; their ceilings are unchanged by flow. Keeping one coherent flow entry avoids an artificial loader
between transport, seed semantics and owned replay state.
No core/stage implementation change is part of this feature.

Mesh position, rotation and scale refs cannot be replaced. Assignment throws TypeError
with code `transform` and `Retained vector: use a transform setter` plus the help link.
Use `.set()`, `.setAll()`, components or mesh setters; Camera tuples remain assignable.
Label.position retains its getter-only type and rejects assignment with the same coded
TypeError. Use label.setPosition to validate/copy the new position and stop mesh following.
Labels share the declared math/mat4 dependency; the entry is 5,450 B gzip against
its unchanged 5,546 B ceiling.
The approved test-page 36 guard adds 87 B: core + stage 23,837 to 23,924 B gzip.

Speed work is deferred during Scott's build phase (2026-11-10), with the single
checked-in default in `scripts/speed-phase.json`. Verify, merge and README gates
keep correctness, deterministic work counts and clock/timeout safety checks;
they report deferred benchmarks and timing assertions. The complete inventory
and unchanged budgets are in [speed-phase.md](work-lists/speed-phase.md).
`npm run test:speed` does no measurement while deferred. After Scott ends the
build phase, `MARGO_SPEED_PHASE=active` runs the named suite on a quiet machine,
sequentially with bounded commands. Its entire inventory must pass before release,
along with an empty busy-retest list. Deferral makes no speed or GPU-quality claim. Every build-phase exclusive request
is refused and logged unless the coordinator records Scott's approval for that
exact command with a reason and future expiry in `scripts/gpu-exclusive-allow.json`.
The checked-in allowlist is empty.

New GPU clients retain FIFO admission tickets for shared and exclusive requests.
Detached `gpu-lock.mjs enqueue` submissions retain the 60-minute default gate
wait; `wait <ticket>` observes the same request and never cancels it on timeout.
Status records persist beside the lock, and command logs stay in the submitting
worktree. Older clients remain interoperable but keep their older ordering;
Eligible-lane FIFO applies only to new clients. A shared eligible head request needs one free slot,
not an empty GPU. Commands and observers each have a hard time limit.

Exclusive GPU holds are reserved for classified speed commands or an explicit,
logged timing reason, with a 20-minute maximum including wrapper overhead.
Oversize holds and correctness requests fail before waiting and are recorded in
`test-results/gpu-lock-refusals.log`. Long matrices must release between bounded
suites. This scheduling cap is based on existing 88.4/113.3/184.4-second benchmark
records, not a new measurement on the busy build machine.

GPU scheduling mutexes publish owner identity atomically and reclaim only an
identified dead process. A live or anonymous legacy mutex is never reclaimed by
age; its owner's release is required. Acquisition has a bounded wait (default
60 minutes, `--wait-max` / `MARGO_GPU_WAIT_MAX_MIN`), including mutex contention.
An independent one-second refresh preserves the old reader/writer client's
ten-second freshness convention during synchronous work. Holder/waiter formats
remain compatible. This is CPU-only scheduling evidence, not a GPU speed claim.

Native WebGL2 live rebuild and disposal release the preview renderer's current program before deleting it.
A foreign current program is preserved. The lifetime regression covers both operations and catches a deleted
binding escaping into another plugin's state scope; it adds no rendering feature or timing claim.

Half-float voxel encoding uses one reusable four-byte bit-cast buffer, with no typed-array allocations per voxel.
It retains IEEE binary16 rounding, subnormals and special values. This changes neither brick selection nor the
atlas budget; `tests/f16-allocation.test.js` checks all 65,536 half words, rounding ties and allocation counts.

Voxel streaming memory admission (2026-11-09): `VoxelStreamer.memoryBudget` limits loaded chunk typed-array
bytes, not total process memory. Both ready and loading jobs reserve the loaded chunks' mean size; a finished
stored or generated chunk joins only when its actual `byteLength` fits after LRU eviction outside the load range.
A chunk that cannot fit remains pending, including one larger than the entire budget. Initial unknown-size loads,
pending results, workers, stores and failed saves are outside this budget. Edits, externally added chunks and
budget reductions can leave the protected load range over budget; further admission stops. Deterministic stored,
variable-size and packed-worker regressions are in `packages/voxel/tests/streamer.test.js`.

Biome prefetch shares raw work with streaming and retains at most 1,024 terrain/object results,
with capacity checked on completion. The original 144-tile flight still generates every tile;
all 292 unique default-world worker outputs match the parent exactly. The view entry is
10,454 B gzip, within its unchanged 10,454 B ceiling. The paired proof establishes fewer
requests (view 204 to 144; placement 190 to 144), without a wall-clock speed claim. Evidence:
whitepaper/results/biomes-prefetch-20261109.json and packages/biomes/tests/view-prefetch.test.js.

Windows GPU-lock directory creation waits at most 10 seconds per name when a removed directory is still held
delete-pending. Permanent permission failures and other errors remain failures; ownership and GPU slot limits
are unchanged. `tests/gpu-lock-mutex.test.js` checks a real pending deletion and the failure bound.

The real-data sciviz demos keep a 2 mm, 88 x 128 x 128 CC0 head MRI, one million public-domain 2MASS sources,
and eight daily North Atlantic NOAA wind fields locally in Git LFS. The 2MASS axes are observed RA, Dec and J-Ks
colour, with no inferred distance. Its systematic, truncated sample is biased and not a complete survey.
The wind fields are daily means at 0.995 sigma, not 10 m observations or trajectories; the equirectangular
projection and speed-preserving direction conversion are documented in `examples/assets/sciviz/README.md`.
The MRI intensities are arbitrary scan units. The four older synthetic pages are package test fixtures only.
The demo checks cover 1440 x 900 and 390 x 844 on native WebGPU and forced WebGL2 in Chromium; they do not
establish a new frame-rate, clinical, forecast, browser-family or hardware-tier claim.

Sciviz CPU extraction foundation (2026-11-10): `@margoengine/sciviz/fallback` exports `marchingCubes`, not a
WebGL2 figure adapter yet. The JavaScript entry is 2,002 bytes gzip against a new 2,258-byte ceiling; it loads one
21,851-byte feature-local Rust/Wasm asset on use (24,000-byte test ceiling). Existing entry ceilings are unchanged.
The same derived case table produces normalized positions and unnormalized outward gradients, eight float32
words per vertex, 96 bytes per triangle. Default `maxTriangles` is floor(128 MiB / 96); field, cases, tables and
vertices together are capped at 2 GiB, excluding the returned copy and allocator overhead. Dimensions are at
least two per axis; the input length must match; the level must be finite in float32. Both passes yield every
16,384 cells for cancellation. NaN samples follow the GPU's comparison/interpolation behaviour. All 256 cases,
non-cubic row tails, chunk boundaries and the real MRI are checked in `packages/sciviz/tests/fallback.test.js`.
Root Figure attachment still rejects the engine's WebGL2 preview backend; the optional `sciviz/webgl2`
adapter adds surface and rectangle drawing below. CPU extraction is not integrated into that adapter yet.
Strict surface/rectangle drawing parity passes on Chromium/RTX A6000; the other native layer paths remain pending.

Sciviz native drawing piece (batch 181, 2026-11-10): `await attachWebGL2(engine, { axes: false, ... })`
returns a Figure on a real `backend: 'webgl2'` engine. CPU-backed surfaces, bars, histograms and heatmaps only;
`signal` defaults absent and cancels module waiting/attachment with its exact reason; the module fetch may continue.
no shim, globals or WebGPU device. Root Figure.create remains WebGPU. R32F heights need nx and ny within
MAX_TEXTURE_SIZE and six vertices per cell within a signed GL draw count. The colour map is 256 sRGB8 texels.
Surface uploads use 4 bytes/sample plus 1,024 colour-map bytes; rectangle instance data uses 20 bytes/cell.
No per-cell CPU mesh building is added. The driver shares core depth and respects view viewport/scissor,
restoring GL state after drawing and uploads. Restoration uses retained data, including setHeights' owned copy.
Axes, points/lines, volumes/slices, integrated CPU isosurfaces and the real-data demos are still pending;
unsupported Figure calls reject with coded help before publishing. The browser test's preselected all-pixel
bound is share(d > 2/255) <= 0.001 and mean(max RGB channel difference) <= 0.25/255, at 320 x 240,
single-sampled on Chromium/RTX A6000. All eight images pass, including real context restoration; no
cross-hardware or speed claim. The drawing entry is 4,476 B min+gzip with bare imports external (previously
4,288 B; ceiling 4,442 to 4,476 B), plus the shared Figure root at 36,916 B (previously 36,802 B; ceiling
36,802 to 36,916 B). Scott's optional-package ruling permits these 34 B and 114 B ceiling increases for matching
missing-triangle/boundary-normal correctness and generation-safe GL disposal. Another split would introduce
an artificial shader loader and divide one generation's resource ownership. Readable shaders, full errors and
the existing optional boundary are retained. Core plus stage remains 23,924 B gzip, below the unchanged 25,000 B.
The CPU extractor remains 2,002 B plus its lazy Wasm.

Sciviz restoration (2026-11-10): CPU-backed layers rebuild on a replacement device; `Figure.ready()` waits for
isosurface reconstruction. Pending old-device extractions reject with code `state`. Caller-owned GPU arrays
cannot survive device loss without a CPU copy: their layers hide and must be recreated on the replacement
device. CPU isosurfaces retain 4 bytes per voxel; meshes retain positions, normals and values (28 bytes per
corner), graphs retain 12 bytes per node for positions plus 4 bytes per node value and 8 bytes per edge, and map
tiles retain 4 bytes per decoded pixel for restoration. Bricked volumes reread their source.
3D axis labels use 8 CSS pixels of clearance; crowded tick labels are omitted, with data ticks and grid lines
unchanged. Active bricked frame aborts cancel source signals and late publication; standalone `ready` aborts
cancel only the wait. Regression coverage: `packages/sciviz/tests/restoration-browser.mjs`,
`entries-browser.js`, `updates.test.js` and `demos-browser.mjs` (head/stars at 390 x 844 and 1440 x 900).

Sciviz volume and isosurface grids require integer dimensions of at least two samples per axis; single slices
belong in a 2D `Figure.heatmap`. Axis errors are reported separately from mismatched sample counts.
Overlapping isosurface extractions and bricked frame requests run in request order. An isosurface extraction
holds the displayed and pending vertex buffers (96 bytes per triangle in each); an aborted or failed extraction
keeps the displayed surface. `Figure.replace(old, next)` rebuilds a trace and briefly holds both layers rather
than updating its buffers in place. Await the replacement builder and call `replace` immediately, with no render
or wait between them. Serialize asynchronous changes with `Figure.timeline`; a disposed timeline does not
cancel user callback work. These guarantees are covered by the sciviz unit and browser suites; no speed claim.

Biome whole-world I/O (2026-11-09): the full default 4,096 x 4,096 samples, every PNG/weight
plane/mask/temperature CSV value and saved-world digest match parent 349243b3d. Exports keep
at most one outstanding tile per available worker (one without workers); the paired biome
outputs are requested together, and height-only reads omit unrelated fields. Export tile
requests are 1,024 instead of 1,536 for the documented workload. This proves less repeated
work with identical output; no wall-clock speed ratio or cross-machine deadline is claimed.
The README runner uses one complete page at a time in its one reserved GPU slot, with the

The prebuilt text README atlas is a 48 px/em, 16-pixel-range SDF sample covering printable ASCII
(U+0020 through U+007E). Other characters need another atlas or a runtime Font. Its bitmap generation uses
Chromium's rasterizer, so regenerated bytes can differ by platform/browser version. BMFont loading and rendering
are covered on Chromium; this repair adds no cross-browser or general font-quality claim.

Required test inputs and still-missing real-file proof are listed in
[missing-test-items](work-lists/missing-test-items.md). The fixture gate rejects the audited
skip/early-success patterns in verify; its batch-160 and held-physics exclusions remain explicit.
It does not establish any of the pending real-file, reference-render or hardware claims.

Margo is a small WebGPU engine: core plus the stage facade is 23,950 B gzip (`npm run measure:size` prints the exact figure; the build fails at 25,000 bytes; core alone is 21,584 B of its 21,587 B cap (2026-11-09: core uploads the unit light direction so no shader normalizes that uniform-only value, core 21,553 B to 21,584 B and core + stage 23,924 B to 23,950 B; 2026-11-07: `CADCameraControls` moved to the stage, core 21,586 B to 20,672 B and core + stage 23,013 B to 23,016 B; stable instance rows with changed-row uploads then added 382 B and `Engine.writePoses` 231 B, so core + stage was 23,626 B; CSP diagnostics then added 171 B, taking it to 23,837 B); the 2026-10-30 core cleanup, which removed the view target depth copy pass, `mesh.euler` and four small duplicates, took core from 21,176 B to 20,790 B and core + stage from 22,580 B to 22,189 B; storing a caller's 4x view target depth then added 23 B to each, a package's frame in one render pass 293 B to core + stage, and `Engine.renderTarget` 44 B), and every
other capability is an optional package. That size is a decision, and so are the boundaries below. Each one exists
for one of two reasons: it keeps core small and frozen, or it follows the limits WebGPU guarantees on every adapter
(Margo's device requests none above them, so an app that runs on a laptop also runs on a phone). This page lists every
hard limit, where it starts, what you see when you reach it, and the package or tool that takes you past it.

How to read "Starts at":

- **Enforced**: an exact constant in the source (linked), usually with the test that asserts it.
- **Measured**: a committed result file (linked). Unless a row says otherwise: ASUS Zenbook S 14, Intel Core Ultra 7
  258V with an Intel Arc 140V integrated GPU, Windows 11, Edge 155, AC power, GPU lock held.
- **Not measured**: the boundary exists, but nobody has run the case. No number is given.

Every number here has a row in [whitepaper/claims.md](whitepaper/claims.md) (LIM-001 to LIM-646). Past losses and their
fixes are in [whitepaper/perf-history.md](whitepaper/perf-history.md).

## Scale

| Limit | Starts at | Why | What you see | Escape hatch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Entities (core meshes, assembly nodes included) | Enforced: 8,388,608 slots (2^23; [kernel.ts](../packages/core/src/kernel.ts), [core-dirty-transforms.test.js](../tests/core-dirty-transforms.test.js)). The store starts at `capacity` (default 1,024) and doubles on demand. Measured ([results-scale-node.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/parts/results-scale-node.json), Node 24, quiet-gated): 352.1 B of kernel memory per slot at 1,048,576 slots (351 B by layout); a static kernel tick costs 3.3 ms at 100,006 entities, 20.2 ms at 499,992 and 41.5 ms at 1,000,012. Above 1,048,576 slots: not measured. | One float32 structure-of-arrays Wasm kernel computes every transform, bound and visibility. It is the reason core is small and fast, and its per-entity cost is linear: about 41 ns per entity per frame even when nothing moves. | Growth is automatic. Past the cap `createMesh` throws `RangeError: Capacity`; `Engine.create` with a larger `capacity` throws `RangeError: Capacity: 1..8388608`. A growth that cannot allocate throws and leaves the store as it was. Before the cap, frame time grows with entity count. | `@margoengine/culling`. `CulledInstances` keeps parts out of the entity store entirely: 0.41-0.55 ms CPU per frame at 89,883 parts, flat in part count ([results-culling.json](../examples/package-benchmarks/parts/results-culling.json)); parts lose picking, hierarchy and section caps. `CulledMeshes` GPU-culls parts that must stay core meshes; it removes GPU work, not the kernel tick. |
| Nodes and parts per file in packages | Enforced, default 100,000 ([limits.js](../packages/shared/limits.js), [count-limits.test.js](../tests/count-limits.test.js)): glTF nodes ([gltf](../packages/gltf/src/index.ts), [gltf-pro asset.ts](../packages/gltf-pro/src/asset.ts)), `.margo` nodes ([blender](../packages/blender/src/index.ts)). | Input validation that bounds memory for untrusted files: every node or part becomes a core mesh. | `RangeError: Too many glTF nodes (100001 > 100000; raise the maxNodes option)`; likewise `Too many .margo nodes` (`maxNodes`). | The option the error names, up to core's 8,388,608 entities: `maxNodes` on the glTF, gltf-pro and `.margo` loaders; a value outside 1 to 8,388,608 throws `maxNodes must be an integer from 1 to 8388608`. Load time and memory past 100,000: not measured. |
| Buffers per geometry | Enforced: a geometry's vertex, index and instance buffers (96 B per instance) must each fit the device's `maxBufferSize`; core requests the WebGPU default ([renderer.ts](../packages/core/src/renderer.ts)). Not measured. | WebGPU's guaranteed limits, so the same scene runs on every adapter. | `RangeError: GPU buffer limit` when the geometry is first drawn. | Split the geometry, or draw the copies with `CulledInstances`. |
| Instance rows after culling flips (2026-11-07) | By method: a mesh that culling or `visible` shows takes its batch's next row and one hidden gives its row to the batch's last, so row order inside a batch, and with it draw order among one geometry's instances, follows the order of flips. Proved exact as a set, row for row and in the uploaded GPU rows on 200 random frames of flips and moves ([core-instance-cache.test.js](../tests/core-instance-cache.test.js)) | A one-bit change costs one row (2 map lookups, 24 floats, 96 uploaded bytes), not a full collection and a full upload | Two core meshes of one geometry at exactly the same depth may swap which one shows after a flip. Several cameras on one scene flip most rows and cost what a full collection costs. The WebGL2 renderer still uploads every row each frame | Give coincident surfaces a small offset or separate geometries |
| Failed allocations in core (2026-11-07) | By method: `Engine.retain` makes the instance array and the GPU buffers before it changes anything, and `Renderer.add` frees old buffers only after the new ones exist. Covers what throws: the `GPU buffer limit` check, a failed CPU array, `@margoengine/webgl2-compat/preview`'s GL errors. Proved on a fake device with the real `Engine` and `GPURenderer` ([deep-core-allocation-failure.test.js](../tests/deep-core-allocation-failure.test.js)), and on a real destroyed device in `npm run test:lifecycle:browser` (LIM-330). A failed `rebootDevice` leaves the engine and the canvas on the device they had: the canvas moves last, proved on a real healthy device in the same suite | While a batch grows it holds both sets of buffers, about 1.5 times the new size at the peak. WebGPU reports a real out-of-memory from `createBuffer` asynchronously, not as a throw | A real out-of-memory shows as a `gpu-lost` error on the next frame, with no rollback | Size geometry to the device's `maxBufferSize`; retry a failed `setGeometry` after freeing memory |
| `Picking.pickMany` points per call | Staging memory: 768 bytes a point, freed when the call ends ([picking.ts](../packages/selection/src/picking.ts)). No enforced count. | One 3 x 3 tile a point at WebGPU's 256-byte row pitch. All points read the scene at the call's turn, where separate `engine.pick` calls each read it at their own. | Memory use during a call grows with the number of points, 768 bytes each, until the call ends. | Split a very large list into several calls. |
| Shader variants per engine | Enforced: 64 cached pipeline variants ([renderer.ts](../packages/core/src/renderer.ts)). How close real scenes come: not measured. | Bounds pipeline compilation and memory. Variants come from MSAA, target format and shader text; each pick shader text (`engine.pick` with the scene's pass hooks) is one more. | `RangeError: Shader limit: 64`. | Not needed so far; fewer distinct shader patches per engine. |
| Biome world streaming (`@margoengine/biomes/view`) | Enforced by the check `packages/biomes/tests/flythrough-check.mjs` (run by `check:merge`): a 300 km/h flight over the zero-config world, tiles made by 4 workers as the camera goes, may add at most 0.3 ms to the slowest 1 percent of frames and 1 ms to the worst frame against the same flight with every tile made first; the page spends at most `budget` (default 0.25 ms) a frame sending jobs and copying tiles in. RTX A6000 desktop, Edge 156 headless with `--enable-precise-memory-info`: `performance.memory.usedJSHeapSize` read once per frame, 600 warm-up frames (one of them, 60 before recording, late on purpose: a 200 ms stall, so the floors hold for the steady state after a late frame) then 600 recorded, frames with a garbage collection left out, the median frame, largest of three runs, at the item 53.1 commit (`perf(core, shadows, post)`, 2026-10-29). Per frame, before and after (two steps, item 53.1 parts 1 and 2): three lit meshes 1,428 B to 340 B; 10,000 moving instanced boxes 1,076 B to 292 B; the same room with cascaded shadows and eight moving casters 26,920 B to 860 B; with SSAO, Bloom, tone mapping and FXAA 5,116 B to 1,528 B. The room plus 10,000 `DynamicInstances` boxes (@margoengine/culling), every row rewritten each frame through bulk writes and `update()`, measured 396 B in three runs at the item 53.2 commit (56 B over the room alone, among them the 16 B wrapper of its compute pass). The check fails when a median frame passes these floors; they are only ever lowered. | Every byte a frame allocates is a byte the garbage collector must sweep later, and a collection in the middle of a frame is a stutter. Shadows and post-processing add passes, so they add wrappers. Measured and left as they are: the frame-resources view set clears about 120 B per frame in the post scene (a fix changes the protocol between copies of the resources, judged risky for a frozen core), the SSAO scene walk makes an iterator and an options literal, the fixture setters box about 216 B in the shadowed scene, and each returned WebGPU object costs 16 B. Number boxing in V8's middle tier (Maglev) is gated too: `tests/frame-alloc.test.js` fails a core frame over 780 B, shadows over 620 B and the cascade fit over 128 B there on V8 14 (Node 26) and newer. V8 13 (Node 24, the minimum Node) passes the core limit (628 B) but its Maglev calls Math.sqrt with a boxed argument and result, 32 B a call, so it has its own row for the other two: shadows over 1,120 B (measured 1,081 B, 704 B of it 22 square roots) and the cascade fit over 256 B (measured 242 B, 224 B of it 7 square roots); a square root in JavaScript arithmetic with the same bits would cost every engine more time. Node 22 has no Maglev by default, so the middle-tier probes skip there. A late frame once deoptimized core's frame loop (its delta clamp first ran a compare on a frame past `maxDelta`, with no type feedback), and the loop then ran its next thousands of frames in a tier that boxes numbers: 24 to 84 B more per frame in every scene, seen only when `check:merge` loaded the machine. Fixed in core, and gated twice: the browser check's late warm-up frame, and `tests/frame-alloc.test.js`, which fails when a late frame leaves the loop unoptimized. The Node probes compile on the main thread (`--no-concurrent-recompilation`), so a package build running beside them cannot make them measure a lower tier. `npm run test:frame-alloc:nodes` runs the test on every Node it finds; the probes leave out windows in which V8 collected garbage. In these runs 0 to 3 of 600 recorded frames held a collection. | Keep your own `onFrame` callbacks allocation-free (the check's scenes keep their clock in a `Float64Array`). `node scripts/frame-alloc-browser.mjs --profile --source` names the functions that allocate per frame. |
